2. **No judgmental or ranking-flavored labels.** He rejected the Light / Standard /
   Elevated review tiers. Neutral, descriptive, escalating names work better —
   Level 1 Standard / Level 2 Enhanced / Level 3 Comprehensive Review. He floated
   Basic / Intermediate / Advanced, which reads as sophistication of the
   *technology* rather than depth of *review*.
3. **Name the seniority of the reviewer, not just the office.** For ITS he wanted
   it clear that a supervisory-level person with authority to commit resources is
   involved, not a line technician. Frame this as decision authority the request
   requires, never as competence of the staff.

He also wants Baylor branding carried through headers/footers and draft status
marked on every page.

**Why:** These are tone constraints, not content ones — the same facts land or
fail on phrasing. Getting them wrong costs a full review cycle.

**How to apply:** Before sending any Athletics policy or framework draft for his
review, scan for blame-implying rationale, ranking adjectives on process tiers,
and unqualified office names where seniority matters.

## claude.ai HyperFrames by HeyGen

[HeyGen HyperFrames MCP] — Programmable HTML video projects.

## When to use this MCP

This MCP is the primary HyperFrames surface for hosted chat clients (Claude.ai
web/desktop, ChatGPT, Grok, and similar), where the user has no local filesystem
and the agent cannot author HyperFrames code directly.

From a CLI/IDE agent on the user's machine (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, the
localhost MCP Inspector, etc.), **`compose` and `render_video` are disabled** — these clients have a local
filesystem, so author HyperFrames with the local HyperFrames skills instead, which
produce standalone HTML compositions the user can edit, diff, and commit. Calls to
those two tools from such clients are rejected with a pointer to install them:

    npx skills add heygen-com/hyperframes

The read tools (list_projects, get_project, get_project_status, get_render_status)
stay available to every client.

After installation they expose slash commands like `/hyperframes` (compose),
`/hyperframes-cli` (init, lint, preview, render), and `/hyperframes-media`
(TTS, transcribe, remove-background). See
https://github.com/heygen-com/hyperframes for the full skill list and docs.

But the skills and this MCP are *not* drop-in equivalents:

- Local skills → standalone HTML/GSAP files on disk. No `project_id`, no hosted
  artifact, no integrated cloud render pipeline.
- This MCP → hosted HeyGen project with a `project_id`, a live canvas at
  `app.heygen.com/projects/{id}`, and the cloud render queue.

Route by what the user actually wants:
- "Make a local HTML composition / something I can edit" → use a local skill.
- "Make a HeyGen project I can share / render in the cloud / open in the app"
  → use this MCP, even from a CLI agent.

## What it does

HyperFrames is HeyGen's framework for creating, editing, and rendering programmable
HTML-based video projects. Projects are authored interactively (Magic Edit
chat-driven flow) and rendered to MP4, WebM, or MOV at any framerate. Tools exposed
here cover composing, listing, fetching, and rendering projects… [truncated]

2	
3	[Heading1] What the NCAA Document Says
4	The NCAA Sport Science Institute brought together experts for a summit on performance technologies. The result is a consensus document organized around foundational concepts, recommendations, and implementation strategies. The document boils down to having a written plan. The plan should cover four things: education, data management, technology selection, and continuous improvement.
5	
6	Worth noting:
7	[ListParagraph] The definition of "performance technology" is intentionally broad. If it collects biometric or performance data, it counts. That includes cameras, surveys, and apps, not only wearables.
8	[ListParagraph] Student-athlete rights are front and center. Informed consent, data privacy, and compliance were addressed.
9	[ListParagraph] These tools can cause unintended harm. The document specifically calls out mental health effects: anxiety, fixation on numbers, and body image issues.
10	
11	[Heading1] Five Recommendations
12	Recommendation 1 (Policy) is to have a written plan. Recommendations 2 through 5 are what that plan needs to cover. The table below displays each recommendation and what we should do about it.
13	
14	Recommendation
15	NCAA Strategy
16	Baylor Action Step
17	1. Policy
18	Create a written plan. Build it with a multidisciplinary team (student-athletes, sports medicine, coaches, admin, legal, IT). Review it regularly.
19	Form a MDT (Multi-disciplinary Team) or a Performance Technology Working Group, draft the plan, and present it to S-A Services Staff for input.
20	2. Education
21	Train everyone at least once a year. Tailor content by audience. Cover limitations, data privacy, informed consent, and departmental policies.
22	Add a performance technology module to existing compliance sessions and new student-athletes' onboarding. Different content for coaches, Athletic Medicine, Athletics Performance, and student-athletes, etc.
23	3. Data Management
24	Establish who owns the data, where it lives, who can see it, and what it can be used for. Plan for transfer student-athletes.
25	Run a full technology inventory across all sports. Work with legal and IT to establish ownership, access, and transfer protocols. Develop a data rights/release consent template.
26	4. Tech Selection

28	Build a Technology Evaluation Checklist. Route all new purchases through the Working Group (MDT). Establish a scalable review process with documentation
29	5. Continuous Improvement
30	Collect feedback from student-athletes, coaches, and staff on a regular basis. Student-athlete feedback is not optional. Use it to update the plan.

NCAA Performance Technologies Recommendations

[Heading1] What the NCAA Document Says
The NCAA Sport Science Institute brought together experts for a summit on performance technologies. The result is a consensus document organized around foundational concepts, recommendations, and implementation strategies. The document boils down to having a written plan. The plan should cover four things: education, data management, technology selection, and continuous improvement.

Worth noting:
[ListParagraph] The definition of "performance technology" is intentionally broad. If it collects biometric or performance data, it counts. That includes cameras, surveys, and apps, not only wearables.
[ListParagraph] Student-athlete rights are front and center. Informed consent, data privacy, and compliance were addressed.
[ListParagraph] These tools can cause unintended harm. The document specifically calls out mental health effects: anxiety, fixation on numbers, and body image issues.

[Heading1] Five Recommendations
Recommendation 1 (Policy) is to have a written plan. Recommendations 2 through 5 are what that plan needs to cover. The table below displays each recommendation and what we should do about it.

Recommendation
NCAA Strategy
Baylor Action Step
1. Policy
Create a written plan. Build it with a multidisciplinary team (student-athletes, sports medicine, coaches, admin, legal, IT). Review it regularly.
Form a MDT (Multi-disciplinary Team) or a Performance Technology Working Group, draft the plan, and present it to S-A Services Staff for input.
2. Education
Train everyone at least once a year. Tailor content by audience. Cover limitations, data privacy, informed consent, and departmental policies.
Add a performance technology module to existing compliance sessions and new student-athletes' onboarding. Different content for coaches, Athletic Medicine, Athletics Performance, and student-athletes, etc.
3. Data Management
Establish who owns the data, where it lives, who can see it, and what it can be used for. Plan for transfer student-athletes.
Run a full technology inventory across all sports. Work with legal and IT to establish ownership, access, and transfer protocols. Develop a data rights/release consent template.
4. Tech Selection
Evaluate quality (accuracy, reliability, validity) before you buy. Use evidence-based frameworks. Decisions should be made by a cross-functional group.
Build a Technology Evaluation Checklist. Route all new purchases through the Working Group (MDT). Establish a scalable review process with documentation
5. Continuous Improvement
Collect feedback from student-athletes, coaches, and staff on a regular basis. Student-athlete feedback is not optional. Use it to update the plan.
Annual student-athlete survey. The Working Group runs an annual review. Each technology gets a continuation, modification, or discontinuation decision.

1 BAYLOR ATHLETICS 2 Software and Technology Management Framework 3 <> 4 | Status || Draft for discussion 5 | Date || August 12, 2026 6 | Prepared by || Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics 7 | Responsible offices || Intercollegiate Athletics; Information Technology Services; Office of General Counsel; University Compliance and Risk Services 8 | Review and approval || Business Office and ITS serve as the two control points. Final policy language should be reviewed by the Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, ITS, and Privacy. 9 <
> 10 1. Purpose 11 To increase the efficiency and timeliness of requests for software and technology purchase and implementation, and to establish a consistent, transparent process for how those decisions are made, reviewed, and renewed. 12 1.1 Policy statement 13 Baylor Athletics shall select, acquire, implement, use, access, disclose, retain, and dispose of software, technology, and the data they generate only for authorized athletics, sports medicine, health, safety, performance, compliance, and operational purposes, and only in accordance with Baylor University policies, applicable law, NCAA guidance, contractual obligations, and approved data-governance practices. 14 Software and technology must be governed through a written plan, routine education, defined data rights, structured technology review, and continuous improvement. 15 1.2 Reason for the framework 16 Technology used in athletics may collect biometric, health-related, performance, workload, recovery, video, sensor, survey, software, mobile-application, and other individual-level data. Responsible use of these technologies requires coordination across Athletics, Sports Medicine, Information Technology Services, Privacy, Legal, Compliance, Procurement, and Records Management. 17 This framework is intended to help Baylor Athletics support student-athlete health, safety, privacy, autonomy, data security, and performance while reducing legal, regulatory, contractual, operational, and reputational risk. 18 The framework started with athlete performance technology, which handles the most sensitive data and is subject to the clearest NCAA guidance. It is written to serve as the department's general approach to all technology. The process below applies to every technology request in the department, and the depth of review depends on the request's scope. 19 2. Scope and terminology 20 2.1 Scope 21 Technology refers to tangible items like devices, wearables, equipment, and applications. Software refers to the platforms and systems those items connect to. The two are rarely purchased independently, and this framework covers both. 22 The framework is not limited to performance, health, and wellness. Athlete performance technology sits inside that scope and triggers a review. A request that does not involve any athlete data still goes through the same review mechanism. 23 2.2 Individuals and entities affected 24 [ListBullet] Baylor Athletics staff, coaches, sports medicine personnel, strength and conditioning staff, analysts, administrators, student support staff, and other Baylor personnel who select, use, access, interpret, or disclose technology and the data it generates. 25 [ListBullet] Student-athletes whose data is collected, used, analyzed, inferred, stored, or disclosed through these technologies. 26 [ListBullet] Vendors, contractors, consultants, and other third parties that collect, store, process, analyze, host, transmit, or receive Baylor Athletics data on Baylor's behalf. 27 [ListBullet] Baylor units supporting Athletics, including ITS, Information Security, Office of General Counsel, University Compliance and Risk Services, Privacy, Internal Audit, Procurement, and records-management functions. 28 2.3 Exclusions 29 This framework does not replace or supersede Baylor policies that already govern specific categories of data, systems, conduct, records, or legal obligations. Where a more specific Baylor policy applies, that policy continues to govern. This document should be read as an Athletics-specific overlay that routes technology decisions into existing Baylor governance channels rather than around them. 30 2.4 Definitions 31 <> 32 | Term || Definition for this framework 33 | Technology || Tangible items such as devices, wearables, sensors, cameras, and equipment, together with the applications that operate them. 34 | Software || The platforms and systems that technology connects to, including hosted, cloud, and on-premises applications. 35 | Athlete Performance Technology || Any device, sensor, wearable, software, mobile application, camera, survey, analytics platform, AI-enabled system, or other technology used to collect, infer, monitor, analyze, store, or communicate biometric, performance, workload, recovery, wellness, health, safety, training, competition, or related data about student-athletes. 36 | Athlete Performance Technology Data || Data collected, generated, inferred, stored, analyzed, or disclosed through athlete performance technologies, including performance metrics, physiological metrics, sleep, hydration, nutrition, stress indicators, recovery, training load, practice or game analytics, and related data. 37 | Restricted / Protected Data || Data subject to Baylor data-classification requirements and heightened safeguards, including where applicable PHI, FERPA records, biometric identifiers, credentials, SSNs, financial information, IRB-related research data, and other regulated or sensitive data. 38 | Medical Decision-Making Data || Data used, intended to be used, or reasonably likely to be used to inform medical management, injury evaluation, treatment, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions. 39 | Approved Use Case || A documented and approved purpose, user population, data category, vendor or system, and data lifecycle for a technology. 40 | Student-Athlete Notice || A plain-language explanation to student-athletes of what data is collected, why, who may access it, permissible uses, retention, rights, questions, and concerns. 41 <
> 42 3. Alignment with NCAA guidance 43 The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. That guidance is high-level by design, leaving each school to implement it according to its own needs and resources. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation. 44 4. Intended outcomes 45 [ListBullet] A consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software and technology in use across the department. 46 [ListBullet] Improved utilization of what the department already owns. 47 [ListBullet] Coordinated renewal and term review, giving the department advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to evaluate options well before a renewal decision is due. 48 [ListBullet] Increased staff fluency so that sport administrators and unit staff can address technology questions with confidence. 49 5. Roles and responsibilities 50 The roles below combine the operating roles that move a request through the process with the review functions that must be applied before a request can clear. 51 <> 52 | Role || Responsibility in this framework 53 | Head Coach, Admin, and/or Unit Director || Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the declared data category and proposed review level. 54 | Athletics Executive Sponsor || Owns Athletics operational compliance with this framework and ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved technologies and approved use cases. 55 | Business Office || First control point. Filters all requests before they proceed. Budget, contract, and duplication check process through the Business Office. 56 | ITS / Information Security || Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported. Reviews access, authentication, storage, transmission, monitoring, incident response, and security controls. These requests carry integration, contract, and security implications across departments, so ITS is represented at a supervisory level with the authority to commit ITS resources and to decide on integration and security posture. Technical staff are brought in for specialist review as the request requires. 57 | Director of Applied Performance || Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders. Facilitator, not owner; not the subject-matter expert and not the project manager. 58 | Assigned Project Manager || Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied Performance. 59 | Sport Administrator || Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review. 60 | Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine || Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data. Must be involved where data may inform medical decision-making, injury evaluation, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions. 61 | Athletics Compliance || Coordinates NCAA, conference, student-athlete, and departmental compliance implications. 62 | Office of General Counsel / Privacy || Reviews FERPA, HIPAA, Texas privacy, consent, data rights, disclosure, vendor terms, and legal holds. 63 | Procurement / Contracting || Ensures vendor contracts address ownership, permitted use, storage, access, data sharing, AI training, automated decision-making, downstream sharing, retention, deletion, portability, and breach notification. 64 | Coaches, Staff, and Users || Use technology only for approved purposes, complete required training, avoid unauthorized disclosure, and report suspected misuse or incidents. 65 | Student-Athlete Representatives || Provide feedback on transparency, education, perceived benefits, and potential unintended impacts of technology use. 66 <
> 67 6. Levels of review 68 The level of review depends on three things: what data the technology touches, how many units it serves, and what the department is committing to in cost and contract term. 69 <> 70 | Level || Applies when || Review includes 71 | Level 1Standard Review || No athlete data; single unit; low or one-time cost || Compliance, Privacy, Ownership, Transparency, Interoperability 72 | Level 2Enhanced Review || Performance data, multi-team use, or recurring cost || Full review 73 | Level 3Comprehensive Review || Physiologic or health data; external data sharing; third-party processing of athlete data || Full review, plus data protection review and Health & Wellness / medical sign-off 74 <
> 75 The level is proposed by the requester at intake and confirmed at the control points. 76 7. Exceptions 77 7.1 Urgent and “emergency” requests 78 Urgent requests clear the same control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake to surface issues that would otherwise delay the request: data category, contract term, integration dependency, and whether athlete data leaves Baylor. 79 A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt. This provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis at intake. An expedited request still clears both control points and still carries the review level its data and commitment call for. 80 8. The three phases 81 Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase 82 1.1 A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director. 83 1.2 The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level. 84 1.3 The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point. 85 1.4 The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point. 86 1.5 The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard. 87 1.6 A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons. 88 1.7 The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request. 89 Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use 90 2.1 A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied, depending on the unit and the system. 91 2.2 Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the Director of Applied to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner. 92 2.3 Open requests are tracked as follows: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up. 93 Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision 94 3.1 Review is triggered at six months, or at the end of the competitive season, whichever is longer. Tools used primarily in season are therefore judged on in-season usage. 95 3.2 The review compares actual utilization against the intent stated on the original request. 96 3.3 Low utilization opens a diagnostic conversation before a renewal conclusion. 97 3.4 The outcome is renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue. 98 9. Workflow 99

> 3. Alignment with NCAA guidance The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. That guidance is high-level by design, leaving each school to implement it according to its own needs and resources. This framework is Baylor Athletics' implementation. 4. Intended outcomes [ListBullet] A consistent, shared understanding of the entire inventory of software and technology in use across the department. [ListBullet] Improved utilization of what the department already owns. [ListBullet] Coordinated renewal and term review, giving the department advance visibility of contract end dates and the lead time to evaluate options well before a renewal decision is due. [ListBullet] Increased staff fluency so that sport administrators and unit staff can address technology questions with confidence. 5. Roles and responsibilities The roles below combine the operating roles that move a request through the process with the review functions that must be applied before a request can clear. <> | Role || Responsibility in this framework | Head Coach, Admin, and/or Unit Director || Initiates the request. Completes the Idea Form and internal ATH Form, including the declared data category and proposed review level. | Athletics Executive Sponsor || Owns Athletics operational compliance with this framework and ensures teams, coaches, and staff use approved technologies and approved use cases. | Business Office || First control point. Filters all requests before they proceed. Budget, contract, and duplication check process through the Business Office. | ITS / Information Security || Second control point. Technical, security, and integration review; confirms the system can be supported. Reviews access, authentication, storage, transmission, monitoring, incident response, and security controls. These requests carry integration, contract, and security implications across departments, so ITS is represented at a supervisory level with the authority to commit ITS resources and to decide on integration and security posture. Technical staff are brought in for specialist review as the request requires. | Director of Applied Performance || Single point of contact and facilitator. Holds the weekly standing meeting with ITS and relays status to project managers and stakeholders. Facilitator, not owner; not the subject-matter expert and not the project manager. | Assigned Project Manager || Owns delivery of the individual project. May be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied Performance. | Sport Administrator || Signs off on renewal decisions at Phase 3, informed by the usage review. | Health & Wellness / Sports Medicine || Reviews requests involving physiologic or health data. Must be involved where data may inform medical decision-making, injury evaluation, rehabilitation, or return-to-play decisions. | Athletics Compliance || Coordinates NCAA, conference, student-athlete, and departmental compliance implications. | Office of General Counsel / Privacy || Reviews FERPA, HIPAA, Texas privacy, consent, data rights, disclosure, vendor terms, and legal holds. | Procurement / Contracting || Ensures vendor contracts address ownership, permitted use, storage, access, data sharing, AI training, automated decision-making, downstream sharing, retention, deletion, portability, and breach notification. | Coaches, Staff, and Users || Use technology only for approved purposes, complete required training, avoid unauthorized disclosure, and report suspected misuse or incidents. | Student-Athlete Representatives || Provide feedback on transparency, education, perceived benefits, and potential unintended impacts of technology use. <

> The level is proposed by the requester at intake and confirmed at the control points. 7. Exceptions 7.1 Urgent and “emergency” requests Urgent requests clear the same control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake to surface issues that would otherwise delay the request: data category, contract term, integration dependency, and whether athlete data leaves Baylor. A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt. This provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis at intake. An expedited request still clears both control points and still carries the review level its data and commitment call for. 8. The three phases Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase 1.1 A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director. 1.2 The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level. 1.3 The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point. 1.4 The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point. 1.5 The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard. 1.6 A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons. 1.7 The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request. Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use 2.1 A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied, depending on the unit and the system. 2.2 Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the Director of Applied to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner. 2.3 Open requests are tracked as follows: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up. Phase 3 — Product Review and Renewal Decision 3.1 Review is triggered at six months, or at the end of the competitive season, whichever is longer. Tools used primarily in season are therefore judged on in-season usage. 3.2 The review compares actual utilization against the intent stated on the original request. 3.3 Low utilization opens a diagnostic conversation before a renewal conclusion. 3.4 The outcome is renew, modify or renegotiate, or discontinue. 9. ## Mac ↔ Windows workflow

The good news is you're already in the right place — that folder is *inside* OneDrive, so it syncs to Windows on its own. You don't need to move files anywhere. Most duplication happens when people work around that rather than through it.

**The rules that actually prevent the problem:**

1. **Never download from the OneDrive web UI.** That's the number one duplicate generator — it lands in Downloads, you edit there, and now there are two lineages. Open files in place: `~/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/…` on the Mac, `C:\Users\<you>\OneDrive - Baylor University\…` on Windows. Same file, two paths.

2. **Never have the same .docx open in Word on both machines at once.** Close it on the Mac before you open it on Windows. If both hold it open, OneDrive forks it into a `-DESKTOP-XXXX` conflict copy and you won't notice until the versions have diverged.

3. **Use OneDrive Version History as your undo, not new filenames.** Right-click → Version History works on both platforms. Reserve a new dated filename for the moment a version gets *sent or presented* to someone — like the 08-12 you took into the meeting, and this 08-14. Saving a new file on every edit is what fills a folder up.

4. **Archive superseded versions.** Your folder currently has four parallel 08-12 lineages — `_ER_`, `_MERGED_ER_`, `_WORKFLOW_ER_`, `_EXEC_SUMMARY_ER_` — plus PDFs. That's the shape staleness takes: next week it won't be obvious which one is the trunk. I'd move everything except the current `_ER_2026-08-14` pair and the NCAA source doc into an `_archive/` subfolder. Say the word and I'll do it — I won't touch your files otherwise.

**What's optimal specifically for handing work to me:**

- **I only see the Mac's local copy.** I can't see the OneDrive cloud version or anything on your Windows machine. So the one sequence that burns us is: you edit on Windows → you ask me here before sync lands on the Mac → I silently work from stale bytes and produce a version that quietly drops your Windows edits.
- **The fix is one habit:** after editing on Windows, check the Mac's OneDrive menu-bar icon says "Up to date" before handing me the file. To make this self-checking, I'll state the file's modified timestamp whenever I open one — if it doesn't match your last Windows save, we know sync hasn't landed and I stop.
- **Close the file in Word before asking me to edit it.** Word holds a lock and writes `~$` temp files; my write can fail or get clobbered when Word next saves.
- **I'll keep writing a new dated file rather than overwriting the one you presented.** That's what I did here — the 08-12 you showed in the meeting is byte-for-byte untouched, still 758,981 bytes from Aug 13 16:55.
- Absolute paths and `_YYYY-MM-DD` suffixes are ideal — I can sort and pick the newest without asking you which is current. Spaces and the `__` suffix are fine, they don't cause me trouble.

Assuming you mean on the open items — here's what I'd do, in priority order.

**1. Reply to Kenny today, before v1 is finished.** This is the highest-value move and it's time-sensitive. He asked a yes/no question — are the five components spoken for? — and you now have a document that answers it precisely. Jon's concern about drift away from NCAA compliance is exactly what Appendix A defuses, and it defuses it better *today* as a draft than in three weeks as a finished v1. Send the 08-14 PDF, say all five are mapped, and name the four v1 items outright. Volunteering the gaps is what makes the coverage claim credible. I can draft that reply.

**2. Fix the workflow handout first — it's a five-minute job.** Right now the framework and the standalone handout give different text for step 1.4. If both circulate, someone will notice, and it undercuts the "we have this organized" message. Let me sync it and re-export the PDF before anything goes out.

**3. Soften §3.** The line "That guidance is high-level by design" is the one sentence in the document that can read as downgrading NCAA guidance — and Jon has already reached for the word "required." I'd cut that clause and let the section say the NCAA sets the expectations, each institution implements to its own structure, and this framework is Baylor's implementation. That change costs nothing, asserts nothing about required-vs-recommended that you'd have to defend, and removes the only real hook for Jon's concern.

**4. Form the Working Group before drafting anything else.** This is the structural recommendation. Four of your five v1 gaps — education content, consent template, transfer protocol, annual survey — are all things the Working Group is supposed to produce. Writing them first and forming the group afterward inverts NCAA Recommendation 1 and gives you documents with no owner. Forming the group is also the one item that's purely an organizational decision, not a drafting task, so it's the thing only you and Kenny can unblock. Get names committed, then let the group's first meeting generate the rest. That's a real v1 milestone you can report.

**5. Ask Micah one specific question.** What is the existing institutional intake path for a software or technology request? That single fact is what I had to strip out of Phase 1.4, it's the evidence behind Kenny's "complementary, not separate" position with Jon, and it gives you something concrete to report when Kenny asks about Micah comms — which he explicitly said he wants. One question, one answer, and the framework can state the connection rather than gesture at it.

If you want, I'll do 2 and 3 now — both are small, mechanical, and reversible — and draft the reply in 1 for you to edit. I'd leave 4 and 5 with you since they're conversations, not documents.

Business Office reviews, then ITS. The request is scored against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard and purchased only after both control points are cleared. || Requester initiates; Business Office and ITS are the control points 38:Urgent requests clear the same two control points, with a short risk checklist completed at intake. A request directed by an administrative lead enters the expedited lane on receipt, which provides documentation for what qualifies as urgent, so the distinction does not have to be determined on a case-by-case basis. === WORKFLOW handout: full Phase 1 steps === | Expedited lane || The same gates, plus a short risk checklist completed at intake. A request directed by an administrative lead enters this lane on receipt. | Trial / sandbox || Provisional approval with a hard end date. No physiologic or identifiable athlete data until full approval. | Review trigger || Six months or the end of the competitive season, whichever is longer, so tools used primarily in season are judged on in-season usage. <> The three phases Phase 1 — Proposal, Approval, Purchase 1.1 A request is initiated by the Director of Applied Performance, a Head Coach, or any Admin Unit Director. 1.2 The requester completes the Technology Idea Form and the internal ATH Form. The request must declare its data category and proposed review level. 1.3 The request goes to the Business Office. The Business Office serves as the filter for all requests and the first control point. 1.4 The forms are submitted to ITS for technical, security, and integration review. This is the second control point. 1.5 The request is evaluated against the Technology Evaluation Scorecard. 1.6 A request is disseminated for purchase only after clearing both control points. Declined requests are returned with documented reasons. 1.7 The Director of Applied Performance holds a weekly standing meeting with the ITS representative to review the status of all open requests across all units. The requester may be brought into the meeting where input is needed; their standing attendance is not expected. The Director of Applied Performance provides regular updates on the status of any open request. Phase 2 — Implementation and Product Use 2.1 A project manager is assigned. This may be administrative staff other than the Director of Applied, depending on the unit and the system. 2.2 Status flows from the weekly ITS standing meeting through the Director of Applied to the assigned project manager and stakeholders, so that every open request has a known owner. 2.3 Open requests are tracked as follows: project, item, requester, project manager, date submitted, desired implementation date, current status, and what is holding it up. === framework §3 exact text === 3. Alignment with NCAA guidance The NCAA Sports Science Institute has published guidance on the Responsible Use of Performance Technologies in College Athletics. # Closeout

One command that replaces the manual end-of-day sequence: "any loose ends?" → "commit and push what needs to be" → "is this in memory?" → "write a handoff so Codex can pick this up."

Run all five checks, then give ONE verdict. Do not ask permission between steps — the invocation of this skill IS the authorization for the full sequence (commit+push to KeystoneOS is standing-authorized per `feedback-auto-commit-push`; for any OTHER repo with changes, commit locally and list the push as an open item instead of pushing).

## Step 1 — Loose-ends sweep

- `git status` in every repo touched this session (check cwd first, then any repo mentioned in the conversation; if session context is thin, check `KeystoneOS` and any `DEV/` repo with commits dated today).
- Unfinished todos/tasks from this session (TaskList if available).
- Background jobs or workflows still running.
- Anything the user was promised earlier in the session that wasn't delivered.

## Step 2 — Commit & push

- KeystoneOS: stage, commit with a descriptive message, push. Authorized.
- Other repos with changes: commit locally with a descriptive message; do NOT push without asking — list it in the final report instead.
- Nothing to commit → say so in one line, move on.

## Step 3 — Memory verification

- Check `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/.errors.log` — must be empty. If not, surface contents and fix the hook issue if obvious.
- Confirm today's transcript file exists at `~/.claude/global-memory/transcripts/<today>.md` and was modified within the last few hours.
- If this session produced a durable decision or new active thread, update `~/.claude/global-memory/MEMORY.md` (respect the 2,500-char cap; consolidate before adding) or write a Tier A memory file per the memory-system rules in CLAUDE.md.

## Step 4 — Cross-harness handoff

This is the **canonical durable handoff** — the one future sessions and other harnesses read. (For a mid-session, chat-only summary before `/clear`, that's the `session-handoff` skill; the mattpocock `handoff` skill writes to the OS temp dir and is not durable — don't rely on it for cross-session state.)

If real work happened this session (not just Q&A), write a handoff to
`<repo>/docs/handoffs/<YYYY-MM-DD>-<slug>.md` (or `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/` if no repo fits):

- What was being worked on and why
- Decisions made (with the reasoning that would be lost)
- Exact file paths of everything created or modified this session
- Next actions, most important first
- Anything mid-flight (open questions, awaited inputs)

Plain markdown, no harness-specific syntax — Codex, Antigravity, or a fresh Claude session must be able to resume from it. Commit it with the Step 2 commit when in a repo.

## Step 5 — Verdict

End with a single short report:

```
## Closeout — <date>

**Committed & pushed:** <repos + one-line summary, or "nothing to commit">
**Memory:** captured ✓ / issue found: <what>
**Handoff:** <path, or "not needed — no substantive work">
**Still open:** <numbered list, or "none">

Clear to sign off. / Not clear: <the one thing blocking>.
```

Every file created or modified during the session must appear somewhere in the report with its full path — "where did this save?" should never need to be asked.

## Rules

- Never push to a repo other than KeystoneOS without explicit approval.
- Never skip Step 3 — memory capture failing silently is the user's top recurring worry.
- If a check fails and the fix is quick and safe (restage a file, clear a stale lock), fix it and note it. If the fix is risky, list it under "Still open" instead.
- Total output should fit on one screen. The user is leaving; brevity is the deliverable.

# Handoff — ATH Technology Framework: NCAA crosswalk appendix + document consolidation

**Date:** 2026-08-14
**Owner:** Eric Rash (Applied Performance, Baylor Athletics)
**Predecessor:** `2026-08-13-ath-tech-routing-and-inventory.md`
**Status:** 08-14 document set shipped and internally consistent. Two user-owned
threads in flight (Micah meeting, inventory email). No blockers.

---

## What happened

Kenny Boyd emailed the morning of 8/14 (screenshot in the OneDrive folder). Three asks:

1. Make sure the five NCAA Performance Technologies recommendations are "spoken for"
   in the framework.
2. Build an appendix that shows where — reusing the existing 3-column chart from
   `NCAA_PerformanceTech_v3.docx` with a fourth column carrying the policy reference.
3. Context: Jon felt the 8/13 discussion had veered away from NCAA "required"
   compliance. Kenny's position to Jon is that the ATH/ITS solution must be
   **complementary to the existing ITS/institutional workflow, not a separate one**.
   Kenny wants to be kept updated on Micah comms and pushed toward a version 1.

All three were addressed. The document set was then consolidated to remove
duplicate/stale versions.

---

## Coverage finding (the substantive answer to Kenny)

Verified against the actual text, not recalled:

| NCAA rec | State in the framework |
|---|---|
| 4. Tech Selection | **Fully carried** — §6 review levels, §7 exceptions, §8 Phase 1.2–1.6 incl. Scorecard, both control points |
| 5. Continuous Improvement | **Carried per-technology** — Phase 3.1–3.4 maps ~1:1 onto NCAA's continuation/modification/discontinuation. Annual SA survey + annual plan review absent |
| 3. Data Management | **Largely carried** — §1.1, §2.4, §5 (ITS, OGC/Privacy, Procurement), §6 Level 3. **Transfer student-athletes absent entirely**; no consent/release template |
| 1. Policy | Written plan = the document. **No standing MDT/Working Group; no clause committing the framework to periodic review** |
| 2. Education | **Thinnest** — only "routine education" (§1.1) and "complete required training" (§5). No section, no cadence, no audience tailoring |

Every gap is written into Appendix A as **"planned for Version 1"** — forward-looking,
no blame framing, and **no fabricated section numbers** (a reference that points at
nothing costs a full review cycle with Kenny).

---

## Decisions made (and the reasoning, which would otherwise be lost)

- **Wrote a new dated file rather than editing the 08-12 in place.** The 08-12 was
  presented in the 8/13 meeting and is the copy everyone has. It is byte-for-byte
  untouched (758,981 bytes, Aug 13 16:55).
- **Did NOT name the institutional ITS intake mechanism.** A first draft asserted
  requests "enter ITS through the existing institutional ITS request path." That is
  unverified — nobody has confirmed whether that is ServiceNow, a form, or Micah's team
  directly. Eric explicitly said not to address the mechanism yet. Both the framework
  (Phase 1.4) and Appendix A.2 now state only the *principle* (Athletics steps feed
  that review; they do not create a separate ITS workflow). **Restore the concrete
  mechanism after the Micah meeting.**
- **Rewrote §3.** It previously said NCAA guidance "is high-level by design." With Jon
  already reaching for the word "required," that clause was the one line that reads as
  downgrading NCAA guidance. Now: the guidance "sets the expectations each institution
  is to meet and leaves the method of implementation to the institution," plus a pointer
  to Appendix A. Deliberately makes **no claim about required vs. recommended** — that
  is a factual question about NCAA status that could not be settled from the source docs.
- **The executive summary carried the same "high-level by design" sentence.** Fixed
  there too — fixing it only in the framework would have left it in the 2-page document
  people are most likely to actually read.
- **Kept the exec summary and workflow handout at top level, not archived.** Both are
  dated 08-12 but are the only copy of their respective deliverable; content overlap
  with the framework is 1–3%. Archiving them would have hidden live documents.
- **Preserved the first 08-14 build** in `_Archive/2026-08-14_as-sent/` because Eric had
  already replied to Kenny and may have attached it. That copy still contains the
  "high-level by design" wording.

Tone constraints applied throughout (see Tier A memory
`project_kenny-boyd-doc-review-preferences.md`): no language implying past
incompetence, no ranking-flavored labels, Baylor branding and draft status on every
page.

---

## Files created or modified

All under
`/Users/kristinarash/Library/CloudStorage/OneDrive-BaylorUniversity/00_Primary_Storage_Drive/XXXX_Transfer/SoftwareTechDocs/`

**Current set (all created 8/14):**
- `Software_and_Tech_Management_ER_2026-08-14.docx` — framework, 10 pp, Appendix A
- `Software_and_Tech_Management_ER_2026-08-14.pdf`
- `Software_and_Tech_Management_WORKFLOW_ER_2026-08-14.docx` — handout, 3 pp
- `Software_and_Tech_Management_WORKFLOW_ER_2026-08-14.pdf`
- `Software_and_Tech_Management_EXEC_SUMMARY_ER_2026-08-14.docx` — summary, 2 pp
- `Software_and_Tech_Management_EXEC_SUMMARY_ER_2026-08-14.pdf`

**Archive (created 8/14):**
- `_Archive/README.txt` — describes all three groups
- `_Archive/2026-08-12/` — 8 superseded files, each MD5-verified before and after the
  move. Includes `MERGED_ER_2026-08-12.docx`, confirmed byte-identical in text to
  `ER_2026-08-12__.docx` (pure duplicate).
- `_Archive/2026-08-14_as-sent/` — 2 files, the first 08-14 build

**Also:** `Software_and_Tech_Management_ER_2026-08-12__.pdf` was cloud-only (zero blocks
allocated) and was hydrated to local disk. Everything in the tree is now materialized.

**Build scripts:** `~/.claude/global-memory/handoffs/2026-08-14-ath-tech-scripts/`
(`build_appendix.py`, `build_companions.py`, `docx_full.py`, `topdf_any.scpt`).
These regenerate the 08-14 set from the archived 08-12 source. **They become stale the
moment anyone edits a .docx directly in Word** — re-running would discard that edit.

---

## Folder convention now in force

Current documents live at the top level of `SoftwareTechDocs/`, all sharing one date
suffix. Superseded versions go to `_Archive/<YYYY-MM-DD>/`. `_Archive/README.txt` is
kept current so the folder reads correctly on the Windows side without this
conversation. Do not leave two dates live at the top level.

---

## Next actions, most important first

1. **Micah meeting (Tue or Wed next week)** — Eric reached out 8/14, awaiting a reply.
   Get: (a) the institutional intake path for a software/tech request — this is the
   fact that restores the concrete sentence in Phase 1.4 of *both* the framework and
   the workflow handout; (b) whether ITS already maintains a software/contract
   inventory Athletics can inherit; (c) who at supervisory level attends the weekly
   standing meeting named in §5.
2. **Inventory email to admin unit leaders — Monday 8/17.** Drafted, not sent. Two
   flags raised: (a) tone — an inventory request reads very easily as "you've been
   buying software without oversight," which is exactly the register Kenny cuts; a
   review pass against that was offered; (b) add a line saying the list will be
   cross-referenced with ITS records, so nobody agonizes over completeness and two
   conflicting inventories don't have to be reconciled later.
3. **Form the Working Group before drafting the remaining v1 sections.** Four of the
   five v1 gaps (education content, consent template, transfer protocol, annual
   survey) are things the Working Group is supposed to produce. Drafting them first
   inverts NCAA Recommendation 1 and yields documents with no owner. Forming the group
   is an organizational decision only Eric and Kenny can unblock.
4. **v1 sections, once the group exists:** Education and Training (annual cadence,
   audience-specific), the Working Group charter, transfer-SA data protocol, data
   rights/release consent template, annual SA survey + annual framework review.
   Transfer protocol and consent template need Legal/Privacy input.

---

## Mid-flight / open questions

- Did the reply to Kenny include the first 08-14 PDF? If so, his copy still says
  "high-level by design." Not worth resending on its own — but anything going to **Jon
  or Micah** should be the current build, since that wording is what Jon reacted to.
- Whether NCAA calls this guidance *required* or *recommended* is unresolved and was
  deliberately not asserted anywhere in the documents.
- Uploading ~0.9 MB PDFs to the Claude thread times out when batched; sending them one
  at a time works.
